```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(psych) # Omega
library(lavaan) # CFA analysis
library(mirt) # IRT analysis
library(ggplot2)
library(ggridges) # ridgeline plot
library(ggiraph) # interactive plot
library(ggcorrplot) #corrplot
library(htmlwidgets) # interaction online
```

```{r}
data = read.csv("International_vaiak.csv")
```

# Art Interest

```{r}
data_ai = data %>%
  filter(
    if_any(AI_1_1:AI_2_4, ~ !is.na(.x))) %>%
  mutate(
    Expertise = factor(ArtExp_Expertise_cluster))
```

This graph represent the distribution of the scores of the AI scale. The line in the middle is the Mean.

```{r}

data_ai_score = data_ai %>%
  count(Art_Interest, name = "n") %>%
  filter(!is.na(Art_Interest))

graph_ai = ggplot(data_ai_score, aes(y = n, x = Art_Interest,
                                tooltip = paste0(Art_Interest, ": ", n), 
                                data_id = Art_Interest)) +
  geom_col_interactive(fill = "grey70",
                        hover_css = "fill:#009b64; 
                       stroke:black; 
                       stroke-width:1.5px;") +
  theme_minimal() +
  xlab("Score") + 
  ylab("Frequency") +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
    axis.title.x = element_blank(),
    axis.title.y = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "none") +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = mean(data_ai_score$Art_Interest),
    linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate(
    "text", 
    x = Inf, y = Inf, 
    label = sprintf("Mean = %.2f", mean(data_ai_score$Art_Interest)), 
    hjust = 1.1, vjust = 1.5, 
    size = 4, color = "black") + 
  ggtitle("Art Interest distribution")

girafe(ggobj = graph_ai) 
```

At the end you can find the percentage of responses selected for each items [Here](#answers-for-the-singular-items).

## Internal reliability

```{r, results='hide', fig.show='hide'}
omega_ai = data_ai %>%                              # Omega analysis Art Interest
  select(starts_with("AI")) %>%
  omega
```

We calculate internal reliability with McDonald's $\omega$, which is considered acceptable when above .7. Thus this shows good internal reliability

```{r}
omega_ai$omega.tot
```

## Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA)

For the CFA, I will keep in mind the following criteria: 

- CFI > .9
- TLI > .9
- RMSEA < .8
- SRMR < .8

### One factor model

Firstly, I will carry a one factor model with the additional correlation that we established in the [Introduction](index.html) (Residual correlation between AI_1_3 and AI_1_7; and between AI_2_2 and AI_2_4).

```{r}
Model_AI_one = "interest  =~ AI_1_1 + AI_1_2 + AI_1_3 + AI_1_4 + AI_1_5 + AI_1_6 + AI_1_7 +
                       
                           AI_2_1 + AI_2_2 + AI_2_3 + AI_2_4

                           AI_1_3 ~~ AI_1_7
                           AI_2_2 ~~ AI_2_4" 

AI_onefactor = cfa(Model_AI_one, data = data_ai, std.lv=TRUE, estimator = "MLR")  # CFA with MLR

fitMeasures(AI_onefactor, c(
  "chisq",
  "df",
  "pvalue",
  "cfi",
  "tli",
  "rmsea",
  "rmsea.ci.lower",
  "rmsea.ci.upper",
  "rmsea.pvalue",
  "srmr"))    # Indices
```

The CFI, TLI and SRMR indicate a good fit, while the RMSEA is above the mentioned criteria.

Thus, I present the factor loadings, which I judged keeping the general rule of thumb that a factor loading higher than .70 is excellent and above .50 is good.

```{r}

standardized_results = standardizedSolution(AI_onefactor)

factor_loadings = standardized_results %>%
  filter(op == "=~") %>%
  select(lhs, rhs, est.std, pvalue)

factor_loadings
```

All the items are above .5, but we can notice 4 items below .7: AI_1_1, AI_1_3, AI_1_7, AI_2_1, AI_2_2, AI_2_4. You can find the content of the items [here](#vaiak_items).

Exploring the correlation of the residuals help us understand better the reason. The two empty boxes represent the residuals correlation that are already included in the model.  

```{r}

residuals = residuals(AI_onefactor, type = "cor") # residuals

residuals = residuals$cov

residuals[3,7] = NA

residuals[9,11] = NA

ggcorrplot(residuals,
           lab = TRUE, 
           type = "upper",
           digits = 1,
           show.diag = FALSE,
           ggtheme = theme_void,
           hc.order = FALSE,
           outline.color = "black", 
           colors = c("#6D9EC1", "white", "#E46726")) +
    scale_fill_gradient2(
    limits   = c(-0.4, 0.4),
    midpoint = 0) + 
  ggtitle("Correlations of residual")
```

We notice a higher positive correlation among the AI_2 items compared to the others. This, plus the lower factor loadings of those items seems to suggest than a better model would separate these items from the rests. 

### Two factors model

I proposed a different model, where the two parts of the scale are two separate factors (interest_subjective and interest_behaviour) with a hierarchical higher factor (interest).

```{r}
Model_AI_two = "interest_subj =~ AI_1_1 + AI_1_2 + AI_1_3 + AI_1_4 + AI_1_5 + AI_1_6 + AI_1_7

                interest_beha =~ AI_2_1 + AI_2_2 + AI_2_3 + AI_2_4 

                interest =~ interest_subj + interest_beha" # model

AI_twofactor = cfa(Model_AI_two, data = data_ai, std.lv=TRUE, estimator = "MLR")  # CFA with MLR

fitMeasures(AI_twofactor, c(
  "chisq",
  "df",
  "pvalue",
  "cfi",
  "tli",
  "rmsea",
  "rmsea.ci.lower",
  "rmsea.ci.upper",
  "rmsea.pvalue",
  "srmr"))    # Indices
```

The indexes all improved, but the RMSEA is still above the criteria.

```{r}

standardized_results = standardizedSolution(AI_twofactor)

factor_loadings = standardized_results %>%
  filter(op == "=~") %>%
  select(lhs, rhs, est.std, pvalue)

factor_loadings
```

Here as well all the factor loadings have improved, with AI_1_1, AI_1_3 and AI_1_7 still below .7.

## Item Responce Theory (IRT)

I carry out two distinctive IRT. One for the entire scale, the other with the two subfactors (interest_subjective and interest_behaviour) divided. 

### One factor model

```{r, results='hide', fig.show='hide'}
AI = data_ai %>% 
  select(starts_with("AI"))

AI_grm = mirt(AI, 1, itemtype = "graded") # run the model

coef = coef(AI_grm, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE) # item parameters
```

This graph represent how informative on average the items are in relation to the ability of the participants ($\theta$). The dotted line represents the mean $\theta$. 

```{r}
theta = seq(-5, 5, length.out = 1000)

test_info = testinfo(AI_grm, Theta = theta)/ncol(AI)

df = data.frame(
  theta = theta, 
  information = test_info)

ggplot(df, aes(x = theta, y=information)) +
  geom_line(color = "black", linewidth = 1.2) +
      scale_fill_manual(values=c("black")) +
  ylim(0, 4) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA),
        axis.ticks.length = unit(0.4, "cm"), 
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 15, color = "black"),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 15, color = "black"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 20), 
        legend.position = c(0.20, 0.7),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 14), 
        legend.title = element_text(size = 14), 
        legend.background = element_rect(
          color = "black",  
          linetype = "solid")) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = mean(test_info),
    linetype = "dashed") + 
  annotate(
    "text", 
    x = Inf, y = Inf, 
    label = sprintf("Mean = %.2f", mean(test_info)), 
    hjust = 1.1, vjust = 1.5, 
    size = 4, color = "black") + 
  ggtitle("Information x ability for Art Interest")
```

We can notice that it is in general pretty normally distributed around 0, with a little skewness into the lower values. This means that it is more informative for the people with lower ability. I think it is interesting that is focused that the majority of distribution is below the mean. 

We carried out analysis for the individual items. 

For each item, $a$ represents the discrimination parameter, i.e. how much the value vary in relation to the ability $\theta$. A high $a$ means that the probability of answering an item correctly changes very sharply as $\theta$ increases.

```{r}
coef_item = coef$items

plot_data = data.frame(
  item = rownames(coef_item),
  a = coef_item[, 1])

data.frame(plot_data[, c(1,2)])
```

We can visualize the same data graphically. 

```{r}

ggplot(plot_data, aes(y= a, x = item)) +
  geom_col(color = "black", linewidth = 1.2) +
      scale_fill_manual(values=c("black")) +
  ylim(0, 5) +
  theme_minimal() + 
  ggtitle("Discrimination parameter a of the AI items")
```

We can observe than the items already noticed before (AI_1_1, AI_1_3 and AI_1_7) are the ones with the lower $a$. At the same times, all the items from the AI_2 are also on on the lower parts of the graph.

$b$ represents the how much ability the participants needs to pass from a responce (e.g. 1) to the next (2). For example, in AI_1_1 a participant with an ability of least 0.08802223 (b5) has a 50% probability of responding 6 or higher. The higher the $b$ the more difficult it is.

```{r}
data.frame(coef_item[, 2:7])
```

The graph represents the above shown data. Each box is an item and each line represents the probability to answer in a specific way (P1 probability to answer 1). The slope of the lines represent the $a$, the steeper it is, the higher $a$ is, the more efficient is the question in distinguish between individuals who know the material and those who do not.

```{r}
plot(AI_grm, type = "trace", 
     facet_items = TRUE) # ICCs and category functioning
```

Subsequentially we check how much the factor (Art Interest) is linked to the item. $F1$ represents the factor loading, while $h2$ is how much variability of the item is explained by the factor.

```{r}
summary(AI_grm) # threshold check
```

## Distribution

Following Anna Panzeri adviced for the CFA I plan 15 participants for parameter (11 Factor loadings, 11 Residual variances and 11 Intercepts). Thus I will keep 15 x 33 = 495 participants. 

### Language

```{r}
data_ai_language = data_ai %>%
  group_by(Sett_Language) %>%
  filter(n() > 495) %>%
  ungroup()

summary_ai_language = data_ai_language %>%
  group_by(Sett_Language) %>%
  summarise(
    n_participants = n(),
    art_interest = mean(Art_Interest, na.rm = TRUE),
    art_interest_sd = sd(Art_Interest, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop")

ggplot(data_ai_language, aes(x = Art_Interest, y = Sett_Language, fill = Sett_Language)) +
  geom_density_ridges(scale = 1.8, rel_min_height = 0.01, alpha = 0.8, 
                      quantile_lines = TRUE, quantiles = 2) +
      theme_ridges() + 
  scale_fill_discrete(na.value = "grey70") + 
  ggtitle("AI scores x Languages")

knitr::kable(
  summary_ai_language %>%
  select(Sett_Language, n_participants, art_interest, art_interest_sd), 
  col.names = c("Group", "Number of participants", "Mean", "SD"),
  digits = 2, 
  align = "c")
```

# Extra

## VAIAK items

Answers from 1 (Not at all) to 7 (Very Much)

- AI_1_1 : I enjoyed visiting art classes as a subject in school
- AI_1_2 : I enjoy talking about art with others
- AI_1_3 : I have many friends/acquaintances who are interested in art
- AI_1_4 : I am interested in art
- AI_1_5 : I am always looking for new artistic impressions and experiences
- AI_1_6 : During my everyday life I spontaneously notice art objects that I find fascinating
- AI_1_7 : I come from a family that is interested in art

Answers from 1 (less than once per year) to 7 (once per week or more often)

- AI_2_1 : How often do you visit art museums or art galleries on average?
- AI_2_2 : How often do you read books, magazines or catalogues about art?
- AI_2_3 : How often do you view images of artworks (picture books, internet, etc.)?
- AI_2_4 : How often do you visit events about art or art history (seminars, projects, festivals, etc.)?
